Código de la Niñez y la Adolescencia, Ley 7739

answers.implementation_then_now: Around January 2023, regular migrants and asylum seekers with a provisional card could join the CCSS. Uninsured adults without status got emergency care, billed afterwards. Children and pregnant women were covered whatever their status, and the ACNUR–CCSS collective-insurance agreement covered a few thousand refugees and asylum seekers a year. The situation was the same around January 2026. The agreement was renewed for 2024 for about 5,000 people (Delfino, Jan. 2024). UNHCR's help portal still describes emergency-only care, billed afterwards, for uninsured people. The CCSS inspection director told La Nación in Dec. 2025 that uninsured people get emergency care and are billed later, and must pay in advance for outpatient care. I found no documented shift within the window. The end of the ACNUR–CCSS agreement (December 2026) falls after the window.

answers.starting_answer_concern: The middle option rests partly on CCSS rules (emergency care for everyone, State insurance for the poor needing an IMAS assessment and an ID document) that were described second-hand and not read in a regulation. The starting answer is plausible but its legal basis for the limits is unread.
answers.notes: No statute, decree or ruling in the window changed migrants' health-care access. Decree 43810 (in force Dec. 2022) delayed asylum seekers' work permits, which indirectly limited contributory insurance; Decree 44501 (2024) undid that. Neither is a cited health provision. The ACNUR–CCSS agreement ends 31 Dec. 2026, after the window, which may matter for later implementation coding. Practice evidence is mostly about refugees and asylum seekers. The La Nación 2025 piece covers uninsured people generally, not migrants specifically. No source specific to irregular labour migrants was read.

provisions.instrument: Reglamento de Operaciones del Sistema Financiero Nacional para la Vivienda (BANHVI)
Reglamento de Operaciones del Sistema Financiero Nacional para la Vivienda (BANHVI)

answers.implementation_then_now: Around January 2023, lawfully settled foreigners received the bono. BANHVI, however, was telling refugees they could not apply: one refusal email was dated 19 January 2023. The Sala Constitucional upheld that refugee's amparo in March 2023 (Semanario Universidad, 24 Mar. 2023; La Teja, 31 Mar. 2023). BANHVI admitted to the Sala that its information was outdated and that including refugees and asylum seekers was legally viable. Around January 2026, BANHVI's own circular, as summarised in the starting answer, admits that improper rejections of refugee applications continued. So the pattern of partial exclusion persisted, and 'Sometimes' holds at both dates. The circular itself is dated 2026, so it falls after 1 January 2026, and I could not open it.

The 2023 Sala ruling is known only from press reports. Its number was not found and it was not read, so it is treated as practice evidence: per the press, it is an order confined to the parties. answers.notes: The 2023 Sala Constitucional amparo (March 2023) falls inside the window. As reported, it is confined to the parties: it voids the email and orders BANHVI not to repeat the conduct. It is not recorded as a legal event and does not change the protection answer. The starting answer's coverage of refugees rests on art. 6 read with DGME's view that refugees have the rights of permanent residents. The BANHVI 2026 circular postdates 1 Jan. 2026, so it does not affect the 2026 answer either way. The practice evidence covers refugees only; nothing was read on regular labour migrants within the window, apart from the 2020 La Nación figure in the starting answer.
